projects.name: HIVE
projects.role: Chief Engineer · built the ROS 2 software stack and designed the rover hardware
projects.summary: A ROS 2 framework that reads a new robot's code, works out what it can do, and runs a mixed robot team from one plain-English mission — end to end in Gazebo.

card.alt: Top-down Gazebo view of the HIVE arena with a quadrotor over the landing pad.

hero.alt: Screen recording of a full HIVE mission: operator dashboard, Gazebo arena, and telemetry.
hero.caption: Full simulation run: “find the red box,” then “bring the red box back to the station” — plans, human approval, and a drone, ground robot, and arm executing in Gazebo with live telemetry.

facts.label: robot types: PX4 quadrotor, TurtleBot3, OpenMANIPULATOR-X

tldr: What: Onboard an unfamiliar robot straight from its ROS 2 workspace, then coordinate a mixed fleet from one natural-language mission.

How: A Composer turns URDF, launch files, and interfaces into a capability descriptor with evidence citations back to the source files; an Executive plans, validates in simulation, waits for human approval, and dispatches to capability-matched agents.
Result: 5 of 5 red-box retrieval missions passed in Gazebo with a quadrotor, a ground robot, and an arm — and the system refuses missions no robot in the fleet can perform.
projects.problem: Every robot in a mixed fleet speaks its own ROS 2 dialect, so adding one usually means weeks of bespoke integration code. HIVE's goal is to replace that with workspace analysis: read the robot's code, derive what it can safely do, and let a single planner coordinate ground, aerial, and manipulator robots from a plain-English mission.

steps.title: Composer reads the robot's code
steps.text: Static analysis of the URDF, launch-file ASTs, message interfaces, and ros_gz bridge config feeds a schema-forced LLM that drafts a Robot Capability Descriptor. Each capability carries evidence citations back to the files it came from.

steps.title: Executive plans and asks for approval
steps.text: The Executive snapshots the fleet, plans against named places, allocates steps by capability, validates the plan in simulation, and stops at a human approve/reject gate before anything moves.

media.alt: HIVE dashboard showing the plan for 'find the red box' with reasoning and Approve/Reject buttons.
media.caption: Operator dashboard: the plan and its reasoning wait at the approval gate.

steps.title: Agents execute with local safety
steps.text: Each robot runs a skill pack chosen by its morphology, with safety limits derived from its capability descriptor. The e-stop lives in a reentrant callback group and polls a cancel token every 0.1 s or faster, so a stop never queues behind a running skill.

media.alt: HIVE dashboard with a scan pattern executing on the drone.
media.caption: A scan pattern running on the quadrotor, tracked live in the dashboard.

steps.title: Mission report and replay
steps.text: Observations fuse into a shared world model, and every run is recorded to MCAP for replay and audit.

media.alt: HIVE dashboard mission report showing all steps complete.
media.caption: Mission report: both steps succeeded in 5 min 01 s.

steps.title: Designing the rover it will run on
steps.text: In parallel I designed a four-wheeled rover with a 5-axis arm on a turntable in Fusion 360 and sized its joints by calculation: the R2b J2 joint needs 56.52 N·m against 80.7 N·m usable inside its enforced workspace limits, and the moving arm came in at 9.28 kg against a 6.7 kg budget — the overrun the next revision has to remove.

media.alt: Fusion 360 render of the HIVE rover with its arm holding a box.
media.caption: Rover design, Ref2 variant (CAD render).

decisions: Provenance is overwritten after the LLM step, so the model can't fabricate its own audit trail — citations come from the static analysis, not from the model.
The planner is allowed to refuse: the Composer benchmark scores calibrated refusal, and a refused plan never reaches the approval gate.
Plans reference named places, never coordinates the LLM invents.
The e-stop runs in a reentrant group with a fast-polled cancel token rather than as a queued action, trading code simplicity for a stop that can't be blocked.
After Gazebo's DetachableJoint failed a one-hour spike, box attachment switched to pose-following — less physical, but reliable enough to test planning.

results.label: red-box missions passed, full tear-down between runs (mean 411 s at real-time factor 0.015–0.037)
halt latency from cruise; drone scan cancel-to-return about 18 ms
tests passing, 0 failures, 2 skipped
robot morphologies identified correctly by the Composer on ground-truthed workspaces

failures.title: Refusing a capability nobody has reviewed
failures.text: When no robot in the fleet holds a reviewed ‘flight’ capability, a mission that needs flight is refused with the reason instead of producing a plan the fleet can’t execute.

media.alt: HIVE dashboard: mission refused because no robot in the swarm has the flight capability required to scan the field.
media.caption: “No robot in the swarm has the ‘flight’ capability required to perform a scan of the field.”

failures.title: Repeatability depends on a fresh stack
failures.text: Missions passed 5/5 on a freshly launched stack but only 3/6 across reset-script sweeps; stale simulator state is the open bug.

failures.title: Benchmark coverage is thin
failures.text: Only 3 of 12 benchmark workspaces are ground-truthed so far, with one model — the Composer numbers are a start, not a verdict.

next: Fix stale-state handling so missions pass on a reset stack, not only a fresh one.
Ground-truth the remaining 9 benchmark workspaces and test more than one model.
Cut the rover arm's mass back under budget, then build and test it with stabilizer feet down for far picks.

projects.name: Natural-language robotic arm
projects.summary: Say or type “put the blue box on the shelf,” and a language agent drives a simulated 7-DOF Franka Panda to do it.

card.alt: Simulated Franka Panda picking up a colored cube in MuJoCo.

hero.alt: MuJoCo recording: a spoken command is transcribed and the Panda places the blue box on the shelf.
hero.caption: Synthesized speech → faster-whisper (local CPU) → agent → simulated Panda. The transcript and its timing on screen come from this run.

facts.label: to transcribe the 2.5 s command in the clip (first call after model load)

tldr: What: A manipulation agent that turns plain-English speech or text into pick-and-place on a simulated Franka Panda.
How: Push-to-talk audio is transcribed locally with faster-whisper, a local parser or NVIDIA NIM tool calling maps it to look/find/pick/place skills, and mink differential IK moves the arm.
Result: Spoken and typed commands drive pick-and-place of four colored cubes, with garbage audio rejected before it can reach the robot.
projects.problem: Language interfaces for robots fail in two dull ways: they hallucinate commands from silence, and they hide the cases where the robot can't do what was asked. The goal was a speech-to-motion loop that runs locally, rejects audio it isn't sure about, and reports failures instead of retrying silently.

steps.title: Listen locally
steps.text: Hold the mic button: audio is recorded at 16 kHz and transcribed on the CPU with faster-whisper (base.en, int8). Nothing is streamed anywhere.

steps.title: Turn words into skills
steps.text: A fast local parser handles common phrasing with no API call; ambiguous requests go to NVIDIA NIM tool calling, which chooses among look, find, pick, and place.

media.alt: Arm control UI with external and wrist camera feeds and a tool-call transcript.
media.caption: Control UI: scene and wrist cameras beside the agent's tool calls.

steps.title: Move with differential IK
steps.text: mink differential IK, with a damped-least-squares fallback, drives the arm to each target pose read from the simulator.

media.alt: MuJoCo recording of typed commands moving cubes onto the shelf.
media.caption: Typed commands, recorded from the simulation: the banner shows the command and the skill running.

steps.title: Grasp and place
steps.text: The gripper closes, a weld constraint attaches the cube, and the arm places it on the shelf.

media.caption: Mid-task: the Panda carrying the red cube.

decisions: Push-to-talk instead of an always-on microphone: the arm only listens when asked, and nothing leaves the machine.

A silence guard before the agent — at least 0.3 s of audio, no_speech_prob ≤ 0.6, avg_logprob ≥ −1.0, and a hallucination blocklist — because Whisper invents words like “Thank you.” on near-silence, and sending those to a robot arm is not acceptable.
Voice is only a new text source; the agent, skills, and simulation stayed untouched, so the speech layer can't break manipulation.
Grasps use a weld constraint rather than contact friction — a deliberate simplification so the work stays on language-to-action, stated openly.

results.label: to transcribe 2.61 s of speech (5.0× real time), base.en int8 on an Intel Core Ultra 9 CPU
to transcribe the 2.5 s spoken command in the clip above, first call after model load
test functions covering recording, transcription gates, and the blocklist

failures.title: Unreachable cubes are reported, not hidden
failures.text: Randomized cubes sometimes land outside the arm's workspace; the agent says so instead of silently retrying.

media.alt: Arm UI showing the error 'Gripper could not reach box_red'.
media.caption: “Gripper could not reach box_red.”

failures.title: Poses come from the simulator
failures.text: Object poses are read as simulator ground truth, not perceived from the cameras — it is a language-conditioned agent over scripted skills, not a vision-language-action model.

next: Estimate object poses from the wrist camera instead of simulator state.
A ROS 2 bridge to drive a physical arm with the same agent.

projects.name: Amphibious ring-frame robot
projects.role: Structural design, component packaging, and the laser-cut frame
projects.summary: One airframe designed to fly, drive, and swim, built around four ring ducts that tilt between flight and driving orientations.

card.alt: Red 3D-printed ring duct around a motor and propeller on its bench mount.

hero.alt: Bench footage of the prototype ring-duct module: a red 3D-printed ring around a motor and propeller on its mount.
hero.caption: Prototype ring-duct module on the bench: 3D-printed ring, motor, and propeller on its mount.

facts.label: domains in one airframe: air, ground, water
frame materials compared in the trade study

tldr: What: A CroLabs robot that uses one structure for flight, driving, and swimming.
How: Four ring ducts with motors and propellers sit on tilt joints around a central electronics bay, tied together by a laser-cut frame.
Result: A ring-duct module and the drivetrain electronics are built for bench testing, and a six-material trade study sets the frame-material path from prototype to flight frame.
projects.problem: A robot that crosses air, ground, and water usually carries three propulsion systems, and the extra mass kills flight time. Tilting ring ducts let the same motors and structure serve every mode — which puts the whole burden on a frame that must be light, stiff, waterproof, and survive impacts.

steps.title: Lay out the airframe
steps.text: Four ring frames carry the propellers around a central electronics bay, with servos at each ring's tilt axis.

media.alt: CAD view of the four ring frames, servos, and central deck.
media.caption: CAD layout of the ring frames and central bay.

steps.title: Build the drivetrain on the bench
steps.text: Motors, servos, and the control electronics go together on 3D-printed arms for bench testing.

media.alt: Bench prototype with black 3D-printed arms, motors, servos, and wiring.
media.caption: Bench prototype: printed arms, motors, servos, and control electronics.

steps.title: Build and test the ring-duct module
steps.text: Each ring duct is a 3D-printed ring around a motor and propeller, designed to tilt between flight and driving orientations — the CAD shows both poses.

steps.title: Choose the frame material
steps.text: A trade study scores six sheet materials on stiffness and strength per mass, water durability, impact toughness, in-house manufacturability, and cost, with a sensitivity check on the weights.

decisions: Prototype frames in sealed birch plywood: it has the best bending stiffness per unit mass of the six sheets compared and cuts cleanly on the in-house CO₂ laser.
Move the flight frame to carbon-fiber plate once CNC routing is available — it ranks first whenever machining can be outsourced or water exposure dominates.
Use acetal for splash-zone brackets and parts that take direct hits: it is waterproof, laser-cuttable, and tied with aluminum as the toughest option in a crash.

results.label: ring-duct module and drivetrain electronics assembled for bench testing
sealed plywood's weighted score, first of six at baseline weights
carbon fiber's score when machining is outsourced, first under that weighting

next: Tilt sequencing across all four rings on the full airframe.
Seal the frame and test it in water.

projects.name: Micromouse explorer
projects.summary: A ROS 2 micromouse that gets no map: it senses walls with LiDAR, tracks itself with odometry, builds the maze as it goes, then speed-runs its own learned map.

card.alt: Belief map filling in beside the true maze as the robot explores.

hero.alt: Four synchronized views of one run: belief map, true maze, Gazebo, and RViz.
hero.caption: One closed-loop run, four views: the robot's belief, the true maze, Gazebo, and RViz with the LiDAR scan and odometry trail.

facts.label: moves to search, return, and speed-run a 10×10 maze whose shortest path is 50
coverage on the new pure modules

tldr: What: A micromouse stack where the robot starts with no map and has to discover the maze it is solving.
How: A ray-marched LaserScan feeds a tri-state belief map; flood-fill re-plans after every cell while a ROS 2 controller drives /cmd_vel and closes the loop on /odom in Gazebo Harmonic.
Result: On a seeded 10×10 maze it searches, returns, and speed-runs in 50 moves each — the true shortest path.
projects.problem: The first version solved the maze from a god's-eye view: the planner read the walls from a file and the robot just replayed the answer. It discovered nothing. The rebuild takes the map away — the robot has to sense, believe, and re-plan like a real micromouse.

steps.title: Split what the robot may know
steps.text: The maze generator writes a public spec (size, start, goal — no walls) and a separate truth file. The brain can only read the spec; a test scans the source to prove it never opens the truth.

steps.title: Sense walls
steps.text: A LiDAR node ray-marches the true maze into a real sensor_msgs/LaserScan. The brain waits for a settled scan after every move before updating its belief.

media.alt: Belief map filling in beside the true maze during exploration.
media.caption: Belief (left) versus truth (right) as the explorer searches.

steps.title: Believe and re-plan
steps.text: Every wall is UNKNOWN, WALL, or OPEN. Flood-fill re-runs over the belief after each cell: optimistic while searching, pessimistic for the final speed run.

media.alt: mms view of flood-fill distances and the solved route.
media.caption: Flood-fill distances in the mms simulator.

steps.title: Drive closed loop
steps.text: A cell-motion controller turns each move into /cmd_vel commands and reads position back from /odom, with absolute turn targets anchored from odometry to the world frame.

decisions: Wait for a settled scan, not just the next one — a scan captured mid-move corrupts the map, so the brain checks the robot has stopped before trusting the reading.
Tri-state belief instead of “no wall until seen”: the planner can be optimistic about UNKNOWN while searching and pessimistic before the speed run.
Absolute turn targets anchored once from odometry to the world, so heading errors don't accumulate across turns.
The original omniscient solver stays in the repo as a baseline to compare against.
The ray-cast LiDAR is the default because Gazebo's gpu_lidar publishes nothing without a GPU; lidar:=gz swaps it back.

results.label: search, return, and speed-run moves on a seeded 10×10 maze with a 50-move optimum
moves on the 8×8 four-view run — the true optimum
tests, including a 30-seed maze sweep; 96% coverage on the new pure modules

failures.title: The LiDAR can't prove drift rejection yet
failures.text: The ray-cast sensor uses the controller's own pose estimate, so it can't catch odometry drift — a real sensor model is needed to test that.

failures.title: A blank Gazebo that wasn't a GPU problem
failures.text: Under WSL the 3D view stayed empty. The fix was naming the ogre2 render engine in the world file — not the GPU limitation the design doc had first assumed.

next: Add sensor noise and wheel slip so drift rejection is actually tested.
Run the same brain on a physical micromouse.

projects.name: Robot learning with ACT
projects.summary: A reproducible LeRobot pipeline for SO-101 imitation learning: a 10,000-step ACT run with verified checkpoint reload, and two 80-episode simulated datasets from a scripted expert.

card.alt: Simulated SO-101 arm picking a red cube into a box.

hero.alt: Simulated SO-101 arm performing scripted pick-and-place episodes in MuJoCo.
hero.caption: Scripted-expert demonstrations recorded in MuJoCo for the dataset — demonstrations, not a learned policy.

tldr: What: The toolchain for an imitation-learning study on the SO-101 arm, built so later failures can be blamed on data, not setup.

How: A locked LeRobot 0.5.0 environment on WSL2 and a Blackwell GPU, a measured batch-size probe, bf16 training, a fresh-process reload check, and a MuJoCo scripted expert that writes LeRobot v3 datasets.
Result: 10,000 of 10,000 steps with 0 mismatched tensors on reload, plus 160 checker-passed demonstrations with every failed attempt logged.
projects.problem: Imitation-learning comparisons fall apart when the environment is the variable nobody controls. Before comparing an LLM agent, ACT, and SmolVLA on the same tasks, the setup itself had to be proven — and the comparison protocol frozen before any result existed.

steps.title: Lock the environment
steps.text: uv lockfile, PyTorch 2.10 with CUDA 12.8 for the Blackwell sm_120 GPU, and a CUDA check before anything trains.

steps.title: Probe before training
steps.text: The video decoder path is proven by call counts (34 torchcodec, 0 pyav), and a batch-size probe from 2 to 16 picks the largest safe batch.

steps.title: Train and reload
steps.text: ACT trains for 10,000 steps in bf16; a separate process reloads the checkpoint and runs GPU inference to prove the artifact is usable.

steps.title: Generate demonstrations
steps.text: A MuJoCo scripted expert with mink IK approaches, grasps, transports, and releases; only checker-passed episodes are kept, and every failed attempt is logged with its reason.

decisions: Pick the public dataset by format version, not popularity, so the loader matches LeRobot 0.5.0 exactly.
Batch 12 instead of 16: 16 hit 92% VRAM occupancy and left no room for allocator fragmentation.
bf16 through Accelerate instead of the --policy.use_amp flag, which is inert for training in LeRobot 0.5.0 — 13% less wall-clock time.
Absolute joint targets rather than end-effector deltas for the expert's actions.
Protocol frozen on 2026-08-06 with a dated deviations log, before any result.

results.label: training steps in 4,029 s, exit code 0; 51,597,190 parameters
tensors reloaded / mismatched in the fresh-process check
task-1 expert attempts kept (53%); task 2: 80 of 181 (44%)
expert reachability checks passed

failures.title: Loss isn't success
failures.text: The policy was never evaluated in an environment or on a robot — a final loss of 0.161 says nothing about task success. The work paused in September 2026 before that evaluation.

failures.title: The expert has blind spots
failures.text: Grasps are imposed by a weld, not physically simulated, and the expert covers a subset of the workspace — two of nine grid cells are empty in task 1.

next: Evaluate ACT success rate in simulation against the frozen protocol.
Teleoperated data on hardware, then the SmolVLA comparison.

projects.name: Drone Tracker
projects.role: CAD packaging, component layout, and FEA
projects.summary: A palm-sized ducted quadcopter designed to follow a subject with GPS and film from a tilt gimbal — CAD, packaging, and frame FEA in Fusion 360.

card.alt: Fusion 360 render of the ducted quadcopter with its flight stack and camera gimbal.

hero.alt: Fusion 360 render of the ducted quadcopter with its flight stack and camera gimbal.
hero.caption: Fusion 360 assembly: CINEC 25.1.2 ducted frame with flight stack and camera gimbal.

facts.label: peak von Mises stress, 400 g thrust case

tldr: What: A ~140 mm cinewhoop-style camera drone designed around a SpeedyBee F7 Mini, GPS follow, ELRS control, and a single-axis tilt gimbal.
How: Full packaging in Fusion 360, then a static FEA of the carbon-fiber frame under a 400 g thrust case, comparing frame-only and full-assembly models.
Result: 1.96 MPa peak stress and 1.18 mm max displacement, with the ducts and prop guards shown to carry load alongside the frame.
projects.problem: A palm-sized drone that follows and films someone has to fit a GPS, gimbal, FPV stack, and battery inside roughly 140 mm. The analysis goal was to find where the frame is actually stressed so it can be reinforced or lightened deliberately rather than by guesswork.

steps.title: Package the drone
steps.text: Flight controller, ESC, GPS, receiver, VTX, camera gimbal, and battery are laid out in Fusion 360 around the ducted frame, with every flight-controller port assigned.

media.alt: Top view of the drone CAD assembly.
media.caption: Top view of the assembly.

steps.title: Simplify for analysis
steps.text: About 1,600 bodies are cut down to the structural parts; non-load-bearing electronics come out so bonded contacts don't leave hundreds of unconstrained groups.

steps.title: Apply the load case
steps.text: Carbon fiber, the central top deck fixed, and 0.98 N upward at each motor bell — 400 g total, about twice hover thrust for a ~200 g craft — on a 12 mm tetrahedral mesh.

media.alt: Von Mises stress plot with four upward load arrows and a maximum of 1.955 MPa.
media.caption: Static FEA: central top deck fixed, four upward 0.98 N motor loads, peak 1.96 MPa.

steps.title: Compare frame-only and full assembly
steps.text: A frame-only model shows much higher peak stress than the full assembly: the ducts and prop guards are primary load-sharing members, not just protection.

decisions: Structural-parts-only model: with bonded automatic contacts, keeping the electronics left about 1,596 unconstrained groups.
A 400 g load case — roughly twice hover thrust — as the sizing case for a ~200 g aircraft.
No safety factor reported: the model is isotropic and has no laminate strength data, so a number would be false precision.
Assign every flight-controller port up front: GPS on UART2, ELRS on UART3, VTX control on UART4, gimbal servo on PWM5.

results.label: peak von Mises stress in the full assembly
maximum displacement
weakest zones: prop-guard spokes and duct-to-frame junctions
33-part bill of materials

failures.title: What the model leaves out
failures.text: Linear static only, isotropic carbon fiber, and bonded contacts — impact loads and laminate behavior are not modeled yet.

next: An impact load case for crashes and hard landings.
Print, assemble, and fly; then GPS follow and tracking.

projects.name: Jarvis · agent orchestrator
projects.role: Sole developer of the integration layer
projects.summary: A local-first assistant on OpenJarvis that routes each task to the right model, convenes a three-model council for hard plans, and calls tools over MCP.

card.alt: Jarvis planning council view with three model proposals.

hero.alt: Jarvis agent-graph canvas with connected agent personas.
hero.caption: Agent graph: draw agent-to-agent edges and Jarvis runs them in topological order, at most three at a time.

facts.label: rungs in the model fallback ladder
web tests, network and LLM calls mocked

tldr: What: An assistant that picks a model per task, escalates hard planning to a council, runs user-drawn agent graphs, and calls tools over MCP.
How: A thin FastAPI sidecar wires routing, council, graph, memory, voice, and vision into the OpenJarvis LiteLLM engine without modifying it.
Result: One LLM path with a NIM → NIM → Gemini → Ollama fallback ladder, covered by a 174-test web suite.
projects.problem: Assistants that hard-code one model are brittle: rate limits, outages, and mismatched model strengths all fail the same way. The aim was to integrate existing open-source pieces — wire, don't rewrite — into one assistant that degrades gracefully.

steps.title: One sidecar, one LLM path
steps.text: A FastAPI sidecar connects every feature to the OpenJarvis LiteLLM engine; no model ID is hard-coded.

steps.title: Route and fall back
steps.text: Each task is classified and sent to the best-fit NVIDIA NIM model, falling back to a second NIM model, Gemini Flash, then local Ollama with exponential backoff.

steps.title: Council for hard plans
steps.text: Three model families propose in parallel, a reasoning model critiques, and one plan is synthesized.

media.alt: Council view with three model proposals.
media.caption: Planning council: three proposals, one critique, one plan.

steps.title: Tools and memory
steps.text: MCP servers add a live code knowledge graph, web and GitHub access, and six action tools; durable memory carries facts across sessions.

media.alt: Connections view showing the code graph and routing map.
media.caption: Connections: code knowledge graph and routing map.

decisions: Wire, don't rewrite: OpenJarvis stays vendored and unmodified; the work is integration.
Every LLM call goes through one engine with no hard-coded model IDs, so swapping models is configuration, not code.
Council and agent graph are capped at three concurrent calls to avoid rate-limit storms.
Face enrollment runs landmarks in the browser, and the enrolled vector is never returned to the client.

results.label: web tests across sidecar, router, council, graph, memory, voice, vision, and tools
agent personas available to the graph

failures.title: No routing benchmark yet
failures.text: Latency and routing quality haven't been measured — the fallback ladder is tested for behavior, not for whether it picks the best model.

next: Benchmark routing quality and latency against a fixed task set.
